Coexisting steady-state solutions of a class of reaction-diffusion systems with different boundary conditions

Ningning Zhu1, Dongpo Hu1, Huili Bi2,∗

1 School of Mathematical Sciences, Qufu Normal University, Qufu, Shandong 273165, P.R. China
2 School of Statistics and Data Science, Qufu Normal University, Qufu, Shandong 273165, P.R. China

††footnotetext: ∗ Corresponding author.
E-mail address: bihuili0810@126.com

Key words: Reaction-diffusion system; steady-state; existence; boundary condidtion.

AMS(2020) Subject Classification 35B50; 35J57.

Abstract

In this work, we investigate a reaction-diffusion system in which both species are influenced by self-diffusion. Due to Hopf’s boundary lemma, we obtain the boundedness of the classical solution of the system. By considering a particular function, we provide a complete characterization of the parameter ranges such that coexisting solutions of the system do not exist under three boundary conditions. Then based on the maximum principle, a sufficient condition for the existence of constant coexisting solutions of the system under Neumann boundary conditions was derived.

1 Introduction

In this work, we study the steady-state solutions of the following competing systems with cross-diffusions and self-diffusions,

{∂u∂t=Δ⁡[(d1+a11​u+a12​v)​u]+u⁡(1−u−a1​v),x∈Ω,t>0,∂v∂t=Δ⁡[(d2+a21​u+a22​v)​v]+v⁡(1−a2​u−v),x∈Ω,t>0,α1​u+β1​∂u∂ν=α2​v+β2​∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x)≥0,v(x,0)=v0(x)≥0,x∈Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\Delta[(d_{1}+a_{11}u+a_{12}v)u]+u(1-u-a_{1}v),&~~&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=\Delta[(d_{2}+a_{21}u+a_{22}v)v]+v(1-a_{2}u-v),&~~&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ &\alpha_{1}u+\beta_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\alpha_{2}v+\beta_{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,&~~&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ &u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0,~v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\end{aligned}\right. (1.1)

where Ω⊂ℝn​(n≥1)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}(n\geq 1) is a bounded domain with smooth boundary, and satisfies the interior ball condition at any x∈∂Ωx\in\partial\Omega. uu and vv are the densities of two competing species, αi,βi\alpha_{i},\beta_{i} and ai​j​(i,j=1,2)a_{ij}(i,j=1,2) are nonnegative constants, αi\alpha_{i} and βi\beta_{i} (i=1,2i=1,2) cannot be zero at same time, aia_{i} and di​(i=1,2)d_{i}(i=1,2) are all positive constants, a11a_{11} and a22a_{22} stand for the self-diffusion pressures, while a12a_{12} and a21a_{21} are the cross-diffusion pressures, a1,a2a_{1},a_{2} describe the inter-specific competitions, and d1,d2d_{1},d_{2} are their diffusion rates [19].

In order to analyze and describe the above reaction-diffusion model, it is necessary to clarify the boundary conditions of the region. When αi=0​(i=1,2)\alpha_{i}=0~(i=1,2), we have ∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0, which is called Neumann boundary condition. At this point, individuals who reach the boundary will be reflected back into the region without leaving, meaning that the species is in an isolated environment. When βi=0​(i=1,2)\beta_{i}=0~(i=1,2), we have u=v=0u=v=0. These indicate that individuals who encounter the boundary cross it immediately and thereby maintain the density on the boundary at zero [1]. This means that the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega can effectively absorb all individuals encountering it. Therefore, this boundary is called absorbed, also known as Dirichlet boundary condition. In population dynamics, the Dirichlet boundary condition can sometimes be considered a lethal boundary, because it can be interpreted as meaning that all individuals who encounter ∂Ω\partial\Omega die. When αi,βi>0​(i=1,2)\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}>0~(i=1,2), it is called Robin boundary condition in the mathematical literature.

The system (1.1) was first introduced by Shigesada, Kawasaki and Teramoto in 1979 [14], when they took a nonlinear dispersive force and an environmental potential function into consideration. Since the introduction of the SKT model, numerous experts and scholars have conducted extensive and in-depth research on it. These results mainly include the existence, boundedness and global convergence of classical solutions, the local and global existence of weak solutions, the existence, nonexistence and stability of steady-state solutions, the existence of traveling wave solutions, and so on.

In fact, the study of standard SKT models is quite difficult. More experts and scholars are turning to the study of certain special forms of SKT models. [6, 3, 15, 11] investigated the existence and boundedness of smooth solutions for SKT model without considering self-diffusion effects. Among them, when the spatial dimension is 1 and d1=d2d_{1}=d_{2}, [6] proved the global existence of smooth solutions. Under the same conditions, [15] obtained the uniform boundedness and convergence of smooth solutions. In 2015, Lou and Winkler [11] used the comparison principle and Sobolev regularity theory to obtain the global existence and uniform boundedness of smooth solutions on bounded convex domain when the spatial dimension is less than 3 and d1=d2d_{1}=d_{2}. Taking self-diffusion into consideration, [4] proved the global existence of the unique smooth solution in any spatial dimension; and [7] obtained the global existence of the unique classical solution by using Sobolev embedding theory under the condition of d1=d2d_{1}=d_{2}.

For research on steady-state solutions, one can refer to [12, 5, 8, 9, 10]. By bifurcations and singular perturbation methods, [12] proved the existence of nonconstant positive steady-state solutions for systems on intervals. In 1996, Lou and Ni [8] used the maximum principle and Lyapunov functional theory to prove that in the weak competition case, if self-diffusion and/or cross-diffusion are relatively weaker than diffusion, then there is still no nonconstant steady-state solution. At the same time, they proved that in the weak competition case, with one of the cross-diffusion pressures arbitrarily given but fixed, it is expect to find non-constant steady-state solutions if the other cross-diffusion pressure is large enough [8]. Without considering the influence of self-diffusion, [9] obtained a sufficient condition such that the SKT model has no nonconstant steady-state solutions. When a21=a22=0a_{21}=a_{22}=0, Lou et al. [10] provided the parameters ranges such that the system has no nonconstant positive solutions for a11=0a_{11}=0 and a11≠0a_{11}\neq 0, respectively.

It is obvious to see that the above studies were conducted under Neumann boundary conditions, which is also the most extensively studied scenario. In addition, some scholars have also studied the SKT model under Dirichlet boundary conditions, which can be found in [2, 13, 16, 18] and references therein. The sufficient conditions for the existence of positive steady-state solutions of the system under Dirichlet boundary conditions are given in [13] using the fixed point theory in the case of fixed or sufficiently large cross-diffusion coefficients, respectively. The existence of steady-state solutions for a one-dimensional system was studied using the singular perturbation method [16].

In this work, we consider the following model, which indicates that there are self-diffusions in both competing species and there is no cross-diffusion in either,

{Δ⁡[(d1+a11​u)​u]+u⁡(1−u−a1​v)=0,x∈Ω,Δ⁡[(d2+a22​v)​v]+v⁡(1−a2​u−v)=0,x∈Ω,α1​u+β1​∂u∂ν=α2​v+β2​∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\Delta[(d_{1}+a_{11}u)u]+u(1-u-a_{1}v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &\Delta[(d_{2}+a_{22}v)v]+v(1-a_{2}u-v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &\alpha_{1}u+\beta_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\alpha_{2}v+\beta_{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,&~~&x\in\partial\Omega.\end{aligned}\right. (1.2)

We aim to obtain sufficient conditions such that the system (1.2) has no coexisting solutions under three different boundary conditions, and establish the parameter ranges for the existence of constant coexisting solutions under Neumann boundary conditions. Considering that uu and vv represent species densities, we focus on the nonnegative classical solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.2), which means that (u,v)∈(C1​(Ω¯)∩C2​(Ω))2(u,v)\in(C^{1}(\overline{\Omega})\cap C^{2}(\Omega))^{2}, u,v≥0u,v\geq 0 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega}, and satisfies (1.2) in the pointwise sense.

The remainder of this work is organized as follows. Section 2 gives some basic preliminaries which implies the strict positivity of the nontrivial solutions of system (1.2). In section 3, based on the boundedness of solutions, we obtain two different parameter ranges for nonexistence of coexisting solutions under three boundary conditions. In section 4, we establish the sufficient conditions for the existence of constant coexisting solutions under Neumann boundary conditions.

2 Preliminaries

First of all, we can obtain the positivity of uu and vv in Ω\Omega, which is crucial in subsequent section.

Proposition 2.1.

Let (u,v)(u,v) be a nonnegative classical solution of (1.2). Then if u≢0u\not\equiv 0, we have u>0u>0 in Ω\Omega, and if v≢0v\not\equiv 0, we have v>0v>0 in Ω\Omega.

Proof.

We only prove u>0u>0 in Ω\Omega whenever u≢0u\not\equiv 0, since the positivity of vv in Ω\Omega can be proved in a similar way. Otherwise, there is x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega such that u⁡(x0)=minx∈Ω¯⁡u⁡(x)=0u(x_{0})=\min\limits_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}u(x)=0.

It follows from the first equation of (1.2) that

(d1+2​a11​u)​Δ​u+2​a11​|∇u|2+u⁡(1−u−a1​v)=0.(d_{1}+2a_{11}u)\Delta u+2a_{11}|\nabla u|^{2}+u(1-u-a_{1}v)=0.

Let

L​u=−(d1+2​a11​u)​Δ​u−2​a11​|∇u|2+c​u​with​c=u+a1​v.Lu=-(d_{1}+2a_{11}u)\Delta u-2a_{11}|\nabla u|^{2}+cu~~~{\rm with}~~~c=u+a_{1}v.

Then

c≥0​and​L​u=u≥0​in​Ω.c\geq 0~~{\rm and}~~Lu=u\geq 0~~{\rm in}~\Omega.

So, an application of the strong maximum principle shows that uu is constant in Ω\Omega, and thus u=0u=0, a contradiction to u≢0u\not\equiv 0. This completes the proof. ∎

Remark 2.1.

In the case of Neumann or Robin boundary conditions, we can get further that u,v>0u,v>0 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega} by Hopf’s boundary lemma. In fact, for example, considering the case of Robin boundary conditions, suppose that there is x0∈Ω¯x_{0}\in\overline{\Omega} such that u⁡(x0)=minx∈Ω¯⁡u⁡(x)=0u(x_{0})=\min\limits_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}u(x)=0. If x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega, we can directly derive a contradiction by Proposition 2.1. If x0∈∂Ωx_{0}\in\partial\Omega, then u⁡(x0)<u⁡(x)u(x_{0})<u(x) for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega. Since L​u≥0Lu\geq 0 in Ω\Omega and Ω\Omega satisfies the interior ball condition at x0∈∂Ωx_{0}\in\partial\Omega, it follows from Hopf’s boundary lemma that ∂u∂ν​(x0)<0\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}(x_{0})<0. Hence

α1​u​(x0)+β1​∂u∂ν​(x0)<0,\alpha_{1}u(x_{0})+\beta_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}(x_{0})<0,

a condiction. Therefore, u>0u>0 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega}.

3 Nonexistence of coexisting steady-state solutions

In this section, we will discuss the nonexistence of coexisting solutions for system (1.2) under three different boundary conditions.

3.1 Neumann boundary condition

In this subsection, assume that α1=α2=0\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=0, that is, we consider the following system,

{Δ⁡[(d1+a11​u)​u]+u⁡(1−u−a1​v)=0,x∈Ω,Δ⁡[(d2+a22​v)​v]+v⁡(1−a2​u−v)=0,x∈Ω,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\Delta[(d_{1}+a_{11}u)u]+u(1-u-a_{1}v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &\Delta[(d_{2}+a_{22}v)v]+v(1-a_{2}u-v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,&~~&x\in\partial\Omega.\end{aligned}\right. (3.1)

Firstly, we give the following lemma, which indicates that uu and vv are both bounded.

Lemma 3.1.

Suppose that (u,v)(u,v) is a nonnegative classical solution of (3.1). If u≢0u\not\equiv 0, then u≤1u\leq 1 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. Similarly, if v≢0v\not\equiv 0, then v≤1v\leq 1 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega}.

Proof.

We only prove the boundedness of uu, while the boundedness of vv can be similarly obtained, leaving it for interested readers. Rewrite the first equation of the system (3.1) as follows

{(d1+2​a11​u)​Δ​u+2​a11​|∇u|2+u⁡(1−u−a1​v)=0,x∈Ω,∂u∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &(d_{1}+2a_{11}u)\Delta u+2a_{11}|\nabla u|^{2}+u(1-u-a_{1}v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=0,&~~&x\in\partial\Omega.\end{aligned}\right. (3.2)

Let f⁡(x)=u⁡(x)​(1−u⁡(x)−a1​v​(x))f(x)=u(x)(1-u(x)-a_{1}v(x)), x∈Ωx\in\Omega. Due to Proposition 2.2 in [8], there exist x1,x2∈Ω¯x_{1},x_{2}\in\overline{\Omega} such that

u⁡(x1)=maxx∈Ω¯⁡u⁡(x)≜M,u⁡(x2)=minx∈Ω¯⁡u⁡(x)≜m,u(x_{1})=\max_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}u(x)\triangleq M,~~u(x_{2})=\min_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}u(x)\triangleq m,

and

f⁡(x1)≥0,f⁡(x2)≤0,f(x_{1})\geq 0,~~~f(x_{2})\leq 0,

that is

M⁡(1−M−a1​v​(x1))≥0,m⁡(1−m−a1​v​(x2))≤0.M(1-M-a_{1}v(x_{1}))\geq 0,~~m(1-m-a_{1}v(x_{2}))\leq 0.

Then we have

1−a1​v​(x2)≤m≤u⁡(x)≤M≤1−a1​v​(x1)​ for all ​x∈Ω¯.1-a_{1}v(x_{2})\leq m\leq u(x)\leq M\leq 1-a_{1}v(x_{1})\mbox{~~for~all~}x\in\overline{\Omega}.

Combining this with the nonnegativity of vv, we obtain u≤1u\leq 1 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. ∎

Theorem 3.1.

Suppose that (u,v)(u,v) is a nonnegative classical solution of (3.1). If

(i)​a1>1>a2,d1>d2​ and ​d1≥d2+2​a22\mbox{(i)}~a_{1}>1>a_{2},d_{1}>d_{2}\mbox{~and~}d_{1}\geq d_{2}+2a_{22}

or

(ii)​a1<1<a2,d1<d2​ and ​d2≥d1+2​a11,\mbox{(ii)}~a_{1}<1<a_{2},d_{1}<d_{2}\mbox{~and~}d_{2}\geq d_{1}+2a_{11},

+∇u⋅∇v[(a11u+w1)vu+(−a22v−w2)vu+(a11u+w1+a22v+w2)vu]\displaystyle+\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\Big[(a_{11}u+w_{1})\frac{v}{u}+(-a_{22}v-w_{2})\frac{v}{u}+(a_{11}u+w_{1}+a_{22}v+w_{2})\frac{v}{u}\Big]
=\displaystyle= −|∇u|2(d1+2a11u)v2u2−|∇v|2(d2+2a22v)+2(d1+2a11u)vu∇u⋅∇v\displaystyle-|\nabla u|^{2}\big(d_{1}+2a_{11}u\big)\frac{v^{2}}{u^{2}}-|\nabla v|^{2}\big(d_{2}+2a_{22}v\big)+2(d_{1}+2a_{11}u)\frac{v}{u}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v
=\displaystyle= |∇v|2(−d2−2a22v+d1+2a11u)−(vud1+2​a11​u∇u−d1+2​a11​u∇v)2\displaystyle|\nabla v|^{2}\big(-d_{2}-2a_{22}v+d_{1}+2a_{11}u\big)-\left(\frac{v}{u}\sqrt{d_{1}+2a_{11}u}\nabla u-\sqrt{d_{1}+2a_{11}u}\nabla v\right)^{2}

div[(uv∇w1−uv∇w2+vw1∇u−uw2∇v)vu]<0.\displaystyle\mbox{div}\Big[(uv\nabla w_{1}-uv\nabla w_{2}+vw_{1}\nabla u-uw_{2}\nabla v)\frac{v}{u}\Big]<0. (3.8)

which leads to a contradiction. This completes the proof. ∎

3.2 Dirichlet boundary condition

In this subsection, we consider the case of β1=β2=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0, which leads to the following system,

{Δ⁡[(d1+a11​u)​u]+u⁡(1−u−a1​v)=0,x∈Ω,Δ⁡[(d2+a22​v)​v]+v⁡(1−a2​u−v)=0,x∈Ω,u=v=0,x∈∂Ω.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\Delta[(d_{1}+a_{11}u)u]+u(1-u-a_{1}v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &\Delta[(d_{2}+a_{22}v)v]+v(1-a_{2}u-v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &u=v=0,&~~&x\in\partial\Omega.\end{aligned}\right. (3.9)

Now, we can also deduce that uu and vv are both bounded.

Lemma 3.2.

Suppose that (u,v)(u,v) is a nonnegative classical solution of (3.9). If u≢0u\not\equiv 0, then u≤1u\leq 1 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. Similar, if v≢0v\not\equiv 0, then v≤1v\leq 1 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega}.

Proof.

We only need to prove the boundedness of vv. Proposition 2.1 implies that v>0v>0 in Ω\Omega if v≢0v\not\equiv 0. The second equation of system (3.9) can be transformed into the following form,

{(d2+2​a22​v)​Δ​v+2​a22​|∇v|2+v⁡(1−a2​u−v)=0,x∈Ω,v=0,x∈∂Ω.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &(d_{2}+2a_{22}v)\Delta v+2a_{22}|\nabla v|^{2}+v(1-a_{2}u-v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &v=0,&~~&x\in\partial\Omega.\end{aligned}\right. (3.10)

Suppose on the contrary that there exists a point x0x_{0} such that v⁡(x0)=maxΩ¯⁡v⁡(x)>1v(x_{0})=\max_{\overline{\Omega}}v(x)>1. Obviously, x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega. So we have

Δ​v​(x0)≤0,∇v​(x0)=0​ and ​v​(x0)​(1−a2​u​(x0)−v⁡(x0))≥0.\Delta v(x_{0})\leq 0,~\nabla v(x_{0})=0\mbox{~and~}v(x_{0})(1-a_{2}u(x_{0})-v(x_{0}))\geq 0.

Since v>0v>0 in Ω\Omega, we obtain that 1−a2​u​(x0)−v⁡(x0)≥01-a_{2}u(x_{0})-v(x_{0})\geq 0, that is, 1≥a2​u​(x0)+v⁡(x0)1\geq a_{2}u(x_{0})+v(x_{0}), a contradiction. ∎

Theorem 3.2.

Suppose that (u,v)(u,v) is a nonnegative classical solution of (3.9). If

(i)​a1>1>a2,d1>d2​ and ​d1≥d2+2​a22\mbox{(i)}~a_{1}>1>a_{2},d_{1}>d_{2}\mbox{~and~}d_{1}\geq d_{2}+2a_{22}

or

(ii)​a1<1<a2,d1<d2​ and ​d2≥d1+2​a11,\mbox{(ii)}~a_{1}<1<a_{2},d_{1}<d_{2}\mbox{~and~}d_{2}\geq d_{1}+2a_{11},

then system (3.9) has no coexisting solutions.

Proof.

(i) According to the proof of Theorem 3.1-(i), the following inequality still holds

div[(uv∇w1−uv∇w2+vw1∇u−uw2∇v)uv]>0,\mbox{div}\Big[(uv\nabla w_{1}-uv\nabla w_{2}+vw_{1}\nabla u-uw_{2}\nabla v)\frac{u}{v}\Big]>0,

where w1=d1+a11​uw_{1}=d_{1}+a_{11}u and w2=d2+a22​vw_{2}=d_{2}+a_{22}v.

Now, we consider the following integral

∫Ωdiv[(uv∇w1−uv∇w2+vw1∇u−uw2∇v)uv]dx\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\mbox{div}\left[\Big(uv\nabla w_{1}-uv\nabla w_{2}+vw_{1}\nabla u-uw_{2}\nabla v\Big)\frac{u}{v}\right]\mathrm{d}x
=\displaystyle= ∫∂Ω(u​v​∂w1∂ν−u​v​∂w2∂ν+v​w1​∂u∂ν−u​w2​∂v∂ν)​uv​𝑑S\displaystyle\int_{\partial\Omega}\left(uv\frac{\partial w_{1}}{\partial\nu}-uv\frac{\partial w_{2}}{\partial\nu}+vw_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-uw_{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}\right)\frac{u}{v}\mathrm{d}S
=\displaystyle= ∫∂Ω(a11​u​v​∂u∂ν−a22​u​v​∂v∂ν+v​w1​∂u∂ν−u​w2​∂v∂ν)​uv​𝑑S\displaystyle\int_{\partial\Omega}\left(a_{11}uv\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-a_{22}uv\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}+vw_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-uw_{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}\right)\frac{u}{v}\mathrm{d}S
=\displaystyle= ∫∂Ω(a11​u2​∂u∂ν−a22​u2​∂v∂ν+u​w1​∂u∂ν−(d2​u2v+a22​u2)​∂v∂ν)​𝑑S.\displaystyle\int_{\partial\Omega}\left(a_{11}u^{2}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-a_{22}u^{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}+uw_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-\left(d_{2}\frac{u^{2}}{v}+a_{22}u^{2}\right)\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}\right)\mathrm{d}S.

It is easy to see that the function u2v\frac{u^{2}}{v} in the last term of the integrand doesn’t make sense on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. So in such a case we cannot make calculations directly. Let

Ωε={x∈Ω|dist⁡(x,∂Ω)>ε}​for​any​small​ε>0.\Omega_{\varepsilon}=\{x\in\Omega\big|{\rm dist}(x,\partial\Omega)>\varepsilon\}~~{\rm for~any~small~}\varepsilon>0.

Since (u,v)∈(C1​(Ω¯)∩C2​(Ω))2(u,v)\in(C^{1}(\overline{\Omega})\cap C^{2}(\Omega))^{2}, we observe that

(uv∇w1−uv∇w2+vw1∇u−uw2∇v)uv∈C1(Ωε¯).\big(uv\nabla w_{1}-uv\nabla w_{2}+vw_{1}\nabla u-uw_{2}\nabla v\big)\frac{u}{v}\in C^{1}(\overline{\Omega_{\varepsilon}}).

Then divergence theorem implies that

∫Ωdiv[(uv∇w1−uv∇w2+vw1∇u−uw2∇v)uv]dx\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\mbox{div}\left[\big(uv\nabla w_{1}-uv\nabla w_{2}+vw_{1}\nabla u-uw_{2}\nabla v\big)\frac{u}{v}\right]\mathrm{d}x
=\displaystyle= limε→0∫Ωεdiv[(uv∇w1−uv∇w2+vw1∇u−uw2∇v)uv]dx\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{\Omega_{\varepsilon}}\mbox{div}\left[\big(uv\nabla w_{1}-uv\nabla w_{2}+vw_{1}\nabla u-uw_{2}\nabla v\big)\frac{u}{v}\right]\mathrm{d}x
=\displaystyle= limε→0∫∂Ωε(a11​u2​∂u∂ν−a22​u2​∂v∂ν+u​w1​∂u∂ν−(d2​u2v+a22​u2)​∂v∂ν)​𝑑S.\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{\partial\Omega_{\varepsilon}}\left(a_{11}u^{2}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-a_{22}u^{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}+uw_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-\left(d_{2}\frac{u^{2}}{v}+a_{22}u^{2}\right)\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}\right)\mathrm{d}S.

Let

I1​(ε)=∫∂Ωε(a11​u2​∂u∂ν−a22​u2​∂v∂ν+u​w1​∂u∂ν−a22​u2​∂v∂ν)​𝑑S,\displaystyle I_{1}(\varepsilon)=\int_{\partial\Omega_{\varepsilon}}\left(a_{11}u^{2}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-a_{22}u^{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}+uw_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-a_{22}u^{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}\right)\mathrm{d}S,
I2​(ε)=∫∂Ωεd2​u2v​∂v∂ν​𝑑S.\displaystyle I_{2}(\varepsilon)=\int_{\partial\Omega_{\varepsilon}}d_{2}\frac{u^{2}}{v}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}\mathrm{d}S.

Obviously, I1​(ε)I_{1}(\varepsilon) approaches zero as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0 in terms of Dirichlet boundary conditions. In order to deal with the term I2​(ε)I_{2}(\varepsilon), we write

V={φ(x)∈C1(Ω¯)|φ(x)>0,x∈Ω;φ|∂Ω=0;∂φ∂ν|∂Ω<0}.V=\left\{\varphi(x)\in C^{1}(\overline{\Omega})\big|\varphi(x)>0,x\in\Omega;~\varphi|_{\partial\Omega}=0;~\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\nu}\Big|_{\partial\Omega}<0\right\}.

By Hopf’s Lemma, we have ∂u⁡(x0)∂ν<0\frac{\partial u(x_{0})}{\partial\nu}<0 and ∂v⁡(x0)∂ν<0\frac{\partial v(x_{0})}{\partial\nu}<0 for any x0∈∂Ωx_{0}\in\partial\Omega, and thus u∈Vu\in V and v∈Vv\in V. We now define

g(x):={u⁡(x)v⁡(x),x∈Ω,∂u⁡(x)∂ν/∂v⁡(x)∂ν,x∈∂Ω.\displaystyle g(x):=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{u(x)}{v(x)},~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~&~~x\in\Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial u(x)}{\partial\nu}\big/\frac{\partial v(x)}{\partial\nu},~~~~&~~x\in\partial\Omega.\\ \end{aligned}\right.

Then Lemma 2.4 in [17] shows that g⁡(x)∈C⁡(Ω¯,(0,+∞))g(x)\in C\big(\overline{\Omega},(0,+\infty)\big). Therefore, we conclude that I2​(ε)I_{2}(\varepsilon) also approaches zero as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0. Consequently,

∫Ωdiv[(uv∇w1−uv∇w2+vw1∇u−uw2∇v)uv]dx=0\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\mbox{div}\left[\big(uv\nabla w_{1}-uv\nabla w_{2}+vw_{1}\nabla u-uw_{2}\nabla v\big)\frac{u}{v}\right]\mathrm{d}x=0 (3.11)

thanks to Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem and Dirichlet boundary conditions, a contradiction.

(ii) On one hand, it is obvious to see from Theorem 3.1-(ii) that

div[(uv∇w1−uv∇w2+vw1∇u−uw2∇v)vu]<0,\displaystyle\mbox{div}\Big[(uv\nabla w_{1}-uv\nabla w_{2}+vw_{1}\nabla u-uw_{2}\nabla v)\frac{v}{u}\Big]<0, (3.12)

due to d1<d2d_{1}<d_{2}, d2≥d1+2​a11d_{2}\geq d_{1}+2a_{11} and Lemma 3.2.

Therefore, a contradiction can also be obtained, and the conclusion is valid. ∎

3.3 Robin boundary condition

In this subsection, we consider the following system

{Δ⁡[(d1+a11​u)​u]+u⁡(1−u−a1​v)=0,x∈Ω,Δ⁡[(d2+a22​v)​v]+v⁡(1−a2​u−v)=0,x∈Ω,α1​u+β1​∂u∂ν=α2​v+β2​∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &\Delta[(d_{1}+a_{11}u)u]+u(1-u-a_{1}v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &\Delta[(d_{2}+a_{22}v)v]+v(1-a_{2}u-v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &\alpha_{1}u+\beta_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\alpha_{2}v+\beta_{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,&~~&x\in\partial\Omega,\end{aligned}\right. (3.14)

where αi>0\alpha_{i}>0, βi>0\beta_{i}>0, i=1,2i=1,2.

Lemma 3.3.

Suppose that (u,v)(u,v) is a nonnegative classical solution of (3.14). If u≢0u\not\equiv 0, then u≤1u\leq 1 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega}. Similar, if v≢0v\not\equiv 0, then v≤1v\leq 1 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega}.

Proof.

We only prove the previous statement. First, we can obtain that

{(d1+2​a11​u)​Δ​u+2​a11​|∇u|2+u⁡(1−u−a1​v)=0,x∈Ω,α1​u+β1​∂u∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &(d_{1}+2a_{11}u)\Delta u+2a_{11}|\nabla u|^{2}+u(1-u-a_{1}v)=0,&~~&x\in\Omega,\\ &\alpha_{1}u+\beta_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=0,&~~&x\in\partial\Omega.\end{aligned}\right. (3.15)

Suppose that there exists a point x0∈Ω¯x_{0}\in\overline{\Omega}, such that u⁡(x0)=maxx∈Ω¯⁡u⁡(x)>1u(x_{0})=\max_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}u(x)>1.

(i) If x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega, we have Δ​u​(x0)≤0\Delta u(x_{0})\leq 0, ∇v​(x0)=0\nabla v(x_{0})=0 and u⁡(x0)​(1−u⁡(x0)−a1​v​(x0))≥0u(x_{0})(1-u(x_{0})-a_{1}v(x_{0}))\geq 0. Since u>0u>0 in Ω\Omega, we obtain that 1−u⁡(x0)−a1​v​(x0)≥01-u(x_{0})-a_{1}v(x_{0})\geq 0, that is, 1≥u⁡(x0)+a1​v​(x0)1\geq u(x_{0})+a_{1}v(x_{0}), a contradiction.

(ii) If x0∈∂Ωx_{0}\in\partial\Omega, then u⁡(x0)>u⁡(x)u(x_{0})>u(x) for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega. Thus we can see that ∂u∂ν​(x0)≥0\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}(x_{0})\geq 0. Since u>0u>0 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega} by Remark 2.1, we have

α1​u​(x0)+β1​∂u∂ν​(x0)>0,\alpha_{1}u(x_{0})+\beta_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}(x_{0})>0,

a contradiction. ∎

Theorem 3.3.

Suppose that (u,v)(u,v) is a nonnegative classical solution of (3.14). If

(i)​a1>1>a2,d1>d2,d1≥d2+2​a22,α1≥β1​ and ​α2≤β2\mbox{(i)}~a_{1}>1>a_{2},d_{1}>d_{2},d_{1}\geq d_{2}+2a_{22},\alpha_{1}\geq\beta_{1}\mbox{~and~}\alpha_{2}\leq\beta_{2}

or

(ii)​a1<1<a2,d1<d2,d2≥d1+2​a11,α1≤β1​ and ​α2≥β2,\mbox{(ii)}~a_{1}<1<a_{2},d_{1}<d_{2},d_{2}\geq d_{1}+2a_{11},\alpha_{1}\leq\beta_{1}\mbox{~and~}\alpha_{2}\geq\beta_{2},

then system (3.14) has no coexisting solutions.

Proof.

We only prove the first case. Now, we can still obtain

div[(uv∇w1−uv∇w2+vw1∇u−uw2∇v)uv]>0,\mbox{div}\Big[(uv\nabla w_{1}-uv\nabla w_{2}+vw_{1}\nabla u-uw_{2}\nabla v)\frac{u}{v}\Big]>0,

where w1=d1+a11​uw_{1}=d_{1}+a_{11}u and w2=d2+a22​vw_{2}=d_{2}+a_{22}v.

Notice that ∂u∂ν=−α1β1​u\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=-\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}u, ∂v∂ν=−α2β2​v\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=-\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}v in ∂Ω\partial\Omega. We consider the following integral

∫Ωdiv[(uv∇w1−uv∇w2+vw1∇u−uw2∇v)uv]dx\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\mbox{div}\left[\big(uv\nabla w_{1}-uv\nabla w_{2}+vw_{1}\nabla u-uw_{2}\nabla v\big)\frac{u}{v}\right]\mathrm{d}x
=\displaystyle= ∫∂Ω(a11​u​v​∂u∂ν−a22​u​v​∂v∂ν+v​w1​∂u∂ν−u​w2​∂v∂ν)​uv​𝑑S\displaystyle\int_{\partial\Omega}\left(a_{11}uv\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-a_{22}uv\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}+vw_{1}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}-uw_{2}\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}\right)\frac{u}{v}\mathrm{d}S
=\displaystyle= ∫∂Ω(−a11​α1β1​u2​v+a22​α2β2​u​v2−α1β1​u​v​w1+α2β2​u​v​w2)​uv​𝑑S\displaystyle\int_{\partial\Omega}\left(-a_{11}\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}u^{2}v+a_{22}\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}uv^{2}-\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}uvw_{1}+\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}uvw_{2}\right)\frac{u}{v}\mathrm{d}S
=\displaystyle= ∫∂Ω(−a11​α1β1​u3+a22​α2β2​u2​v−α1β1​u2​w1+α2β2​u2​w2)​𝑑S\displaystyle\int_{\partial\Omega}\left(-a_{11}\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}u^{3}+a_{22}\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}u^{2}v-\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}u^{2}w_{1}+\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}u^{2}w_{2}\right)\mathrm{d}S
=\displaystyle= ∫∂Ωu2​(−a11​α1β1​u+a22​α2β2​v−α1β1​(d1+a11​u)+α2β2​(d2+a22​v))​𝑑S\displaystyle\int_{\partial\Omega}u^{2}\left(-a_{11}\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}u+a_{22}\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}v-\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}(d_{1}+a_{11}u)+\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}(d_{2}+a_{22}v)\right)\mathrm{d}S
=\displaystyle= ∫∂Ωu2​(−2​a11​α1β1​u+2​a22​α2β2​v−d1​α1β1+d2​α2β2)​𝑑S\displaystyle\int_{\partial\Omega}u^{2}\left(-2a_{11}\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}u+2a_{22}\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}v-d_{1}\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}+d_{2}\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}\right)\mathrm{d}S
≤\displaystyle\leq ∫∂Ωu2​(−2​a11​α1β1​u+2​a22​α2β2−d1​α1β1+d2​α2β2)​𝑑S\displaystyle\int_{\partial\Omega}u^{2}\left(-2a_{11}\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}u+2a_{22}\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}-d_{1}\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}+d_{2}\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}\right)\mathrm{d}S
≤\displaystyle\leq ∫∂Ωu2​(−2​a11​α1β1​u+2​a22−d1+d2)​𝑑S\displaystyle\int_{\partial\Omega}u^{2}\left(-2a_{11}\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}u+2a_{22}-d_{1}+d_{2}\right)\mathrm{d}S
≤\displaystyle\leq 0,\displaystyle 0,

due to α1≥β1\alpha_{1}\geq\beta_{1}, α2≤β2\alpha_{2}\leq\beta_{2} and d1≥d2+2​a22d_{1}\geq d_{2}+2a_{22}, a contradiction.

4 Existence of coexisting solutions

In this section, we will investigate the existence of coexisting solutions for system (3.1).

Theorem 4.1.

Let a1<1a_{1}<1 and a2<1a_{2}<1. Suppose that (u,v)(u,v) is a nonnegative classical solution of (3.1). If u≢0u\not\equiv 0 and v≢0v\not\equiv 0, then

u≡1−a11−a1​a2​and​v≡1−a21−a1​a2.\displaystyle u\equiv\frac{1-a_{1}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}~~~\mbox{and}~~~v\equiv\frac{1-a_{2}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}. (4.1)
Proof.

By Lemma 3.1, there exist x1,x2∈Ω¯x_{1},x_{2}\in\overline{\Omega} such that

u⁡(x1)=maxx∈Ω¯⁡u⁡(x)≜M,u⁡(x2)=minx∈Ω¯⁡u⁡(x)≜m,u(x_{1})=\max_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}u(x)\triangleq M,~~u(x_{2})=\min_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}u(x)\triangleq m,

and

1−a1​v​(x2)≤m≤u⁡(x)≤M≤1−a1​v​(x1)​ for all ​x∈Ω¯.\displaystyle 1-a_{1}v(x_{2})\leq m\leq u(x)\leq M\leq 1-a_{1}v(x_{1})\mbox{~~for~all~}x\in\overline{\Omega}. (4.2)

Similarly, there exist x3,x4∈Ω¯x_{3},x_{4}\in\overline{\Omega} such that

v⁡(x3)=maxx∈Ω¯⁡v⁡(x)≜M′,v⁡(x4)=minx∈Ω¯⁡v⁡(x)≜m′,v(x_{3})=\max_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}v(x)\triangleq M^{\prime},~~v(x_{4})=\min_{x\in\overline{\Omega}}v(x)\triangleq m^{\prime},

and

1−a2​u​(x4)≤m′≤v⁡(x)≤M′≤1−a2​u​(x3)​ for all ​x∈Ω¯.\displaystyle 1-a_{2}u(x_{4})\leq m^{\prime}\leq v(x)\leq M^{\prime}\leq 1-a_{2}u(x_{3})\mbox{~~for~all~}x\in\overline{\Omega}. (4.3)

We first prove u≡1−a11−a1​a2u\equiv\frac{1-a_{1}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}. Combining (4.2) with (4.3), we obtain

m≥1−a1​v​(x2)≥1−a1​(1−a2​u​(x3))≥1−a1+a1​a2​m,\displaystyle m\geq 1-a_{1}v(x_{2})\geq 1-a_{1}(1-a_{2}u(x_{3}))\geq 1-a_{1}+a_{1}a_{2}m, (4.4)

and

M≤1−a1​v​(x1)≤1−a1​(1−a2​u​(x4))≤1−a1+a1​a2​M.\displaystyle M\leq 1-a_{1}v(x_{1})\leq 1-a_{1}(1-a_{2}u(x_{4}))\leq 1-a_{1}+a_{1}a_{2}M. (4.5)

Notice that since a1<1a_{1}<1 and a2<1a_{2}<1, we have

1−a11−a1​a2≤m≤u⁡(x)≤M≤1−a11−a1​a2.\displaystyle\frac{1-a_{1}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}\leq m\leq u(x)\leq M\leq\frac{1-a_{1}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}. (4.6)

Hence

u≡1−a11−a1​a2.u\equiv\frac{1-a_{1}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}.

Similarly, it can be proved that

1−a21−a1​a2≤m′≤v⁡(x)≤M′≤1−a21−a1​a2.\displaystyle\frac{1-a_{2}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}\leq m^{\prime}\leq v(x)\leq M^{\prime}\leq\frac{1-a_{2}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}. (4.7)

Consequently,

v≡1−a21−a1​a2.v\equiv\frac{1-a_{2}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}}.

This completes the proof. ∎
